summary: This RFC discusses subsets of the Unicode character repertoire for use in protocols and data formats, and specifies three subsets recommended for IETF specifications.

eli5.summary: Unicode has a huge number of characters, and some are risky. This picks three smaller, safer collections.

questions: which unicode characters should specs allow
what are problematic unicode code points
what is the difference between xml characters and unicode scalars
subtitle: Three named subsets of Unicode that protocols can cite to keep out surrogates, stray control codes and noncharacters.

tldr.problem: The set of all Unicode code points is a poor choice for text fields, because it includes surrogates, legacy control codes and noncharacters that cannot be used for interoperable interchange.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines three increasingly restrictive subsets, Unicode Scalars, XML Characters and Unicode Assignables, each given in ABNF, so other specifications can cite one by name.
tldr.outcome: Protocol authors can restrict text fields in formats such as JSON to one of these subsets. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has no IANA actions.

today: RFC 9839 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2025. It has not been obsoleted or updated, so it is the current reference for these three subsets.

sections.title: Why Specify a Subset
sections.content:
Protocols and data formats often carry text made of Unicode characters. Each character has a numeric code point, but not every code point is appropriate in protocols, and some are not even associated with characters. So even if the goal is to support "all Unicode characters", a subset of the code point repertoire should be specified.

This document discusses the issues, names two subsets that have been popular in practice, and suggests one new subset. The intended use is as a cross-reference target for other specifications that want to exclude problematic code points. The RFC only covers code points that cannot be used for interoperable interchange. Language, text direction and alternate representations of the same character are left to efforts such as PRECIS (RFC 8264).

Numeric values are written in hexadecimal with Unicode's U+ notation, such as U+0041 for "A". Ranges are inclusive, and in ABNF (RFC 5234) hexadecimal values are written with %x.
sections.eli5: If you let anyone write anything in a form, some strange characters can break it. This RFC gives a short list of safe sets of characters to choose from.

sections.title: Code Points and Problematic Ones
sections.content:
There are 1,114,112 code points (17 * 2^16). As of Unicode 16.0 (2024), about 155,000 are assigned to characters. Because unassigned code points regularly become assigned, it is usually not a good practice to specify that unassigned ones should be avoided. The RFC also notes that RFC 2277 says protocols MUST be able to use UTF-8, which becomes a mandate to use it where a single encoding form is specified.

The RFC calls a code point problematic if it is a surrogate, a noncharacter, or a legacy control. Private-use code points are not classed as problematic, since they may be used by private agreement.

  • Surrogates: 2,048 code points in U+D800-U+DFFF, used in pairs in UTF-16. A surrogate in any other encoding form has no meaning, and UTF-8 forbids representing one.
  • Control codes: 65 code points in U+0000-U+001F, U+0080-U+009F and U+007F. Newline (U+000A), carriage return (U+000D) and tab (U+0009) are the "useful controls". The rest are "legacy controls" and are mostly obsolete.
  • Noncharacters: the last two code points of each of the 17 planes (U+FFFE, U+FFFF, U+1FFFE and so on up to U+10FFFF) and the range U+FDD0-U+FDEF.
sections.eli5: Some Unicode slots are half pieces that only work in pairs, some are old machine commands, and some are marked "never use for sharing". Those are the problem slots.

sections.title: Dealing with Problematic Input
sections.content:
Noncharacters and legacy controls are unlikely to cause software failures, but they cannot be usefully displayed to humans and can be used in display-based attacks. Software behavior on surrogates is unpredictable and differs between programming languages, even between API calls in the same language.

If input were always well-formed UTF-8, implementors would never meet surrogates. In practice problematic code points do occur where the input source is not controlled by the implementor. JSON (RFC 8259) allows any code point in member names and string values, so the RFC shows a conforming JSON text whose value holds a NUL, a C1 control, an unpaired surrogate and a noncharacter. It cannot be serialized to well-formed UTF-8, and libraries handle it unpredictably.

Two reasonable options are rejecting text with problematic code points or replacing them with placeholders, ideally U+FFFD. Silently deleting an ill-formed part of a string is a known security risk. RFC 9413 discusses strategies for such input in more depth.
sections.eli5: When a weird character shows up, you can either refuse the whole message or swap the weird character for a clear stand-in mark. Quietly throwing it away is the risky choice.

sections.title: The Three Subsets
sections.content:
The three subsets are increasingly restrictive, and specifications can refer to them as "Unicode Scalars", "XML Characters" and "Unicode Assignables". Each is given as an ABNF production.

Unicode Scalars is every code point except the surrogates. It is the default for CBOR (RFC 8949). It excludes surrogates but still includes legacy controls and noncharacters.

XML Characters comes from the Char production in XML 1.0 (Fifth Edition). It excludes surrogates, legacy C0 controls and the noncharacters U+FFFE and U+FFFF. It does not exclude all problematic code points; the RFC argues C1 controls are less likely than C0 controls to appear in error, and noncharacters above U+FFFF are rarely encountered.

Unicode Assignables is the new subset: all code points that are not problematic. It is a proper subset of each of the others, and covers all currently assigned code points except legacy controls, plus those that might be assigned in the future.
sections.eli5: There are three sieves. The first catches only the half pieces, the second also catches some old commands, and the third catches all the bad pieces.

sections.title: Using the Subsets
sections.content:
Many IETF specifications rely on formats such as JSON, I-JSON, CBOR, YAML and XML, and these formats come with default subsets. JSON, for example, allows all problematic types in member names and string values. A JSON-based protocol can be made more robust by restricting those fields to one of the subsets, and equivalent restrictions are possible for the other formats.

Escaping cannot be used to get around such a restriction. The restriction applies to the data content, not to its textual representation in the packaging format. If a JSON field were restricted to Unicode Assignables, the RFC's example would remain valid JSON but the data it represents would not be Unicode Assignable.
sections.eli5: A rule about which characters are allowed applies to the real letters, not to a disguise. Writing a banned character in code form does not make it allowed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security discussion is mostly in the section on problematic input. The RFC points to Unicode Security Considerations (TR36) and Unicode Source Code Handling (TR55) as wide-ranging surveys, noting that many attacks aim to deceive human readers but issues with surrogates and noncharacters can contribute to such exploits. The security considerations of RFC 8264 generally apply as well.

Because the three subsets omit more and more problematic code points, they should be less and less susceptible to these exploits, and Unicode Assignables excludes all of them. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: The smaller the set of allowed characters, the fewer tricks an attacker has. The strictest of the three sets leaves out all the known problem characters.
